entities.name: Fianna Fáil
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Fianna Fáil ('Soldiers of Destiny'), founded in 1926 by Éamon de Valera after his split from Sinn Féin over the Anglo-Irish Treaty, was the dominant party in Irish politics from 1932 to 2011 — governing Ireland for more than 60 of those 79 years and shaping the country's conservative Catholic social policy, protectionist economics, and republican nationalist identity. De Valera's 1937 Constitution — which gave special recognition to the Catholic Church, banned divorce and contraception, and defined women's role as domestic — shaped Irish society until the liberal reforms of the 1990s.

De Valera founded Fianna Fáil as the 'slightly constitutional' alternative to Sinn Féin — accepting parliamentary politics while maintaining republican principles. The party's first government (1932) reversed the pro-British policies of the Cumann na nGaedheal government by abolishing the oath of allegiance to the British crown, withholding land annuities, and entering an 'Economic War' with Britain. De Valera's 1937 Constitution established Ireland as a sovereign state in fact if not yet in name (formal Republic declared 1948).

Fianna Fáil's long dominance — 16 unbroken years (1932-1948), then alternation with Fine Gael — ended catastrophically with the 2007-2010 financial crisis, when a construction bubble inflated by Fianna Fáil's light-touch regulation burst. GDP fell 14%, unemployment trebled, and Ireland required an EU-IMF bailout of €85 billion. The 2011 election reduced Fianna Fáil from 77 to 20 seats — the worst electoral collapse of any governing party in Irish history. Fianna Fáil's recovery and 2020 coalition with its historic rival Fine Gael marked a pragmatic end to the Civil War-era political divide.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Fianna Fáil's 1937 Constitution — which embedded Catholic social teaching into Irish law and shaped the country's social conservatism for 60 years — and its catastrophic 2011 collapse after causing Ireland's financial crisis define the rise and fall of 20th-century Irish political nationalism.
